content.title: About
content.content: Avocado is the edible fruit of the avocado tree (Persea americana), native to Central and South America and now cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. The fruit has a creamy texture, a mild buttery flavor, and is rich in healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Avocado is sometimes called the "fruit butter" because of its smooth texture.
It contains more monounsaturated fat than olive oil.
Inside each fruit is a large seed that can be roasted and eaten.
One avocado provides over 10% of the daily recommended potassium intake.
There are more than 500 avocado varieties, with Hass being the most common.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: These fats help lower LDL cholesterol and support heart health.

items.title: High potassium content
items.content: Potassium aids blood pressure regulation and muscle‑nerve function.

items.title: Source of vitamins E and C
items.content: Antioxidant vitamins protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to avocado.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite its benefits, avocado is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: People with sensitive stomachs may experience discomfort when consuming large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Avocado is eaten raw: sliced into salads, spread on toast, blended into smoothies, used in guacamole, or as a mayo substitute. A ripe fruit yields to gentle pressure; if it’s too firm, let it ripen at room temperature.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unripe avocados at room temperature until they soften. Once ripe, store them in the refrigerator for up to 3–5 days. To slow browning, drizzle cut pieces with lemon juice.

content.title: About
content.content: Carrot juice, 100% is a pure juice extracted from fresh carrots without added sugars, preservatives or flavorings. It has a bright orange colour, a mildly sweet taste and the characteristic aroma of carrots.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrot juice is rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A.
The deep orange colour comes from high levels of carotenoids.
It is often used in baby foods because of its gentle flavour and nutritional value.
In the 19th century carrot juice was promoted as a remedy for improving eyesight.
The juice can be frozen while retaining most of its nutrients.

items.title: Supports vision
items.content: Beta‑carotene, converted to vitamin A, is essential for retinal health and night vision.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin C help neutralise free radicals, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune system support
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immune response and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Skin health
items.content: Vitamin A and antioxidants promote skin renewal and may improve appearance.

items.title: Reduced risk of chronic diseases
items.content: Phytochemicals in carrots may help lower the risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: High natural sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, the natural sugars can raise the glycemic index, which is relevant for diabetics.

items.title: Loss of dietary fiber
items.content: Juicing removes much of the fiber, so juice does not replace whole carrots in the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled, add it to smoothies, cocktails, sauces or soups. To balance sweetness, mix with a splash of lemon juice or ginger.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container for up to 3‑5 days. Freeze in airtight containers for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate candy with a cookie filling consists of bite‑size sweets coated in milk or dark chocolate and filled with a soft, crumbly cookie mixture. They offer a sweet, creamy chocolate flavor combined with a tender, slightly crunchy cookie interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recipe for chocolate candy with a cookie filling appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
The filling typically contains butter, sugar, vanilla and finely crushed cookie pieces.
These candies are popular as holiday gifts, especially for New Year’s and Valentine’s Day.
In different countries the filling may be enriched with nuts, caramel or fruit bits.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate, especially dark, provides flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Contains simple carbohydrates that can quickly replenish energy stores.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium present in cocoa supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: The candies contain milk chocolate, which can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: A large amount of sugar may contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of tooth decay.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Cocoa contains small amounts of caffeine, which should be considered for children and caffeine‑sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the candies as a standalone snack, add them to dessert assortments, or use them as decorative elements in baked goods. Keep them dry to prevent the chocolate from melting.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep them refrigerated to prevent chocolate bloom.

content.title: About
content.content: Fresh coconut is the mature fruit of the coconut palm (Cocos nucifera) grown in tropical regions. Inside is fragrant, slightly sweet flesh and refreshing coconut water. Coconut is eaten raw, used in cooking, cosmetics, and traditional medicine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A coconut palm can live over 80 years and produce fruit for up to 30 years.
Inside a coconut are three main products: coconut water, flesh, and oil.
Coconut water is rich in electrolytes and is often used as a natural sports drink.
Coconut flesh contains about 33 % saturated fat, mainly lauric acid.
Historically, coconut was a vital source of drinking water and food for sailors.

items.title: Rich in electrolytes
items.content: Coconut water provides potassium, sodium, magnesium, and calcium, helping maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Heart support
items.content: Lauric acid in the flesh may help raise HDL (good) cholesterol levels.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Coconut contains phenolic compounds that act as antioxidants.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Fiber in the flesh promotes intestinal motility and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Coconut-derived substances have antimicrobial properties.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Large portions of coconut flesh can increase overall calorie and saturated fat intake.

items.title: Acidity of coconut water
items.content: People with sensitive stomachs may feel discomfort after excessive consumption of coconut water.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Open a fresh coconut, drink the water, and cut the flesh into cubes to add to salads, smoothies, desserts, or make coconut milk. The flesh can also be dried and eaten as a snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep a whole coconut in a cool, dry place for up to 2–3 weeks. Once opened, store the flesh in an airtight container in the refrigerator and use within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: A doughnut is a deep‑fried piece of dough, typically round with a hole in the center. The “cake type” variant has a denser, cake‑like crumb, and the icing adds a sweet glaze and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts appeared in Europe in the 17th century and quickly became popular in the United States.
The classic American cake‑type doughnut is made from a yeasted batter but without a central hole.
Icing can be chocolate, vanilla, caramel, or flavored with fruit purées.
In Japan, “mochi‑donut” uses glutinous rice instead of wheat flour.
Some countries fill doughnuts with jam, custard, or cream.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Doughnuts provide a quick boost of energy thanks to their carbohydrate content, making them a convenient snack.

items.title: Protein content
items.content: Egg‑ and milk‑based batter supplies a modest amount of protein useful for muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain thiamine, niacin, and folate, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Small amounts of iron, magnesium, and phosphorus are present.

items.title: Mood uplift
items.content: The sweet taste and aroma can improve mood and reduce stress.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Glaze and dough make doughnuts calorie‑dense and can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Deep‑frying can create trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The batter often contains eggs, milk, and wheat—common allergens.

items.title: Excess calories
items.content: Regular consumption may contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy doughnuts while they are still warm. They are commonly paired with coffee or tea. Icing can be topped with nuts, coconut flakes, or powdered sugar for extra texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, keep refrigerated, though the crust may lose its crispness.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-no.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with meat, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled egg with meat prepared without added fat is a dish made from eggs and lean meat (such as chicken breast or turkey). Eggs provide high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins and minerals, while the lean meat adds extra protein, iron and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most nutrient‑dense foods with a high biological value.
Cooking without added fat preserves the natural taste of the ingredients and reduces the calorie count.
Meat in the dish increases satiety and provides a slower release of energy.
Traditionally omelets are cooked with a little oil, but a non‑stick pan or steaming can be used to avoid added fat.
The dish is commonly included in the diets of athletes and people monitoring fat intake.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs and lean meat together supply all essential amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain B12, riboflavin (B2) and biotin, while meat provides niacin (B3) and B6, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Meat adds iron and zinc; eggs contribute phosphorus and selenium, supporting immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low in added fats
items.content: The absence of added oil makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of protein and the small amount of natural fat in eggs helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Use lean, fresh meat without excessive salt or preservatives.

items.title: Spoilage
items.content: Fresh meat and eggs should be stored at ≤4 °C and used within a few days.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs, stir in finely chopped lean meat, season with salt and pepper. Pour the mixture onto a pre‑heated non‑stick pan with no oil, cook over medium heat, gently stirring until the eggs set but remain tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a pan without adding fat.

content.title: About
content.content: Pie with peanut butter cream is a dessert consisting of a tender crust, a layer of smooth peanut butter cream, and often topped with glaze or nut crumbs. The peanut butter cream gives a sweet, nutty flavor and creamy texture, while the crust provides a light, crisp bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanut butter cream is usually made from roasted peanuts, sugar, and oil, sometimes with a pinch of salt for balance.
Nut‑filled pies are popular in the United States, often served at holidays and family gatherings.
The contrast between sweet crust and slightly salty peanut butter cream is a favorite among dessert lovers.
Some recipes add chocolate or caramel to the cream for an extra rich taste.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Peanut butter cream provides a notable amount of protein, important for tissue repair.

items.title: Healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Peanuts are rich in monounsaturated fats that may support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanuts contain niacin, folate, and vitamin B6, which play roles in energy metabolism.

items.title: Magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals help maintain normal muscle and bone function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Resveratrol and other phytochemicals in peanuts help combat free radicals.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are a strong allergen; individuals with peanut allergy may experience severe reactions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Pie with peanut butter cream is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sugar in the crust and cream can raise blood glucose levels; people with diabetes should limit intake.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Some recipes add salt to the cream, which may be a concern for those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pie as a dessert with tea or coffee, cut into portions, and keep refrigerated. It can also be gently warmed in the microwave to soften the cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the pie in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze it wrapped in plastic film and foil; thaw at room temperature before serving.

rice-white-with-cheese-and-or-cream-base.title: White Rice with Cheese and/or Cream Based Sauce, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: This is boiled white rice served with a sauce made from cheese and/or cream that is prepared without added fat. The rice provides a light, neutral base, while the sauce adds a gentle creamy flavor without extra calories from fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is one of the most widely consumed grains worldwide.
A fat‑free creamy sauce is made from low‑fat cottage cheese, skim milk, or plant‑based alternatives.
Such dishes are common in dietetic menus and for people monitoring their fat intake.
Rice is easily digestible and often used in therapeutic diets for gastrointestinal issues.
Combining rice with cheese improves calcium bioavailability.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates, useful for post‑exercise recovery.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce adds calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Protein
items.content: The cheese sauce supplies a modest amount of complete protein, aiding tissue repair.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cheese sauce may contain lactose, which can cause discomfort for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy proteins should avoid this sauce.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, so portion control is important for people with diabetes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the sauce is seasoned with salt, total sodium intake should be monitored.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice hot, drizzled with the cheese or cream sauce. Garnish with fresh herbs, green onions, or spices to taste. The dish works as a main course or as a side to lean meat or fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Store the sauce separately in a sealed container, also for up to 3 days. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

rice-white-with-peas-and-carrots-ns-as-t.title: Rice, white, with peas and carrots

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, white, with peas and carrots is a ready‑to‑eat dish that combines boiled white rice, green peas, and carrots. It is a nutritious and balanced meal often served as a side or light lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of rice, peas, and carrots offers a variety of flavors and textures.
The dish is traditionally popular in Asian and Mediterranean cuisines.
Peas provide a good source of plant protein, while carrots are rich in beta‑carotene.
It can be easily prepared at home and stored in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.
Variations may include spices such as turmeric or cumin to enhance flavor.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: White rice supplies energy through slowly digestible carbohydrates.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas add a significant amount of protein beneficial for muscles and tissues.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Carrots contain vitamin A (beta‑carotene), vitamin K, and potassium, supporting vision and immunity.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from peas and carrots promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The dish contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: High glycemic index of rice
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium content in prepared dish
items.content: If seasoned with salt, total sodium intake should be considered.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a standalone meal, a side to meat or fish, or incorporate into salads. Add soy sauce, herbs, or spices for extra flavor if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze for up to 2 months, thawing in the fridge before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Flavored sunflower seeds are roasted sunflower kernels coated with natural flavorings (e.g., barbecue, smoky, cheese). They have a crunchy texture, a light salty note, and a pronounced taste characteristic of the chosen flavor. Seeds are commonly eaten as a snack, added to salads, yogurts, and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sunflower is one of the fastest‑growing crops; a single plant can reach up to 3 m in height within a season.
Sunflower seeds are rich in vitamin E, magnesium, and selenium.
Flavorings are usually made from natural extracts of spices, herbs, and dried fruits, without artificial colorants.
In Russia and other CIS countries, flavored seeds became a popular street snack in the 2000s.
Sunflower seeds are also processed into oil, which is considered one of the healthiest vegetable oils.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat is polyunsaturated, including omega‑6, which is important for heart health.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Seeds deliver plant protein and dietary fiber, helping to promote satiety.

items.title: Supports skin health
items.content: Vitamin E and fatty acids help keep skin moisturized and protected.

items.title: Seed allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to sunflower seeds.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Seeds are calorie‑dense, so they should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Salt and flavor additives
items.content: Excessive salt or artificial additives can be undesirable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Risk of over‑snacking
items.content: Because they are easy to eat, flavored seeds can lead to overeating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Seeds can be enjoyed straight from the bag, tossed into salads, soups, yogurts, porridge, or used in baking. They are often lightly roasted to enhance flavor. For lower sodium intake, choose unsalted versions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.

tuna-noodle-casserole-with-cream-or-whit.title: Tuna Noodle Casserole with Cream or White Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna noodle casserole with cream (or white) sauce is a classic American comfort dish that became popular in the mid‑20th century. It combines cooked egg noodles, canned tuna, vegetables (often peas and carrots), and a rich sauce made from cream, milk, or cheese, resulting in a hearty and flavorful casserole.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the 1950s as an inexpensive, quick family dinner.
Canned tuna provides a high amount of protein and omega‑3 fatty acids, making the casserole nutritionally dense.
Traditional recipes often top the casserole with breadcrumbs or grated cheese for a crunchy crust.
A white sauce (béchamel) version is lighter, while a cream‑based sauce yields a richer, richer flavor.
Tuna noodle casserole is a staple in school cafeterias and camp menus as a comforting, easy‑to‑prepare meal.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Tuna supplies all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s promote heart health and help reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins source
items.content: Vitamin B12 and B6 in tuna aid nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from the sauce
items.content: Creamy or cheese‑based sauces increase calcium and vitamin D content, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Carbohydrates from noodles
items.content: Egg noodles provide quick‑release energy, useful after physical activity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium varieties if you have hypertension.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Tuna may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Saturated fat levels
items.content: Cream sauces and cheese add saturated fats, which should be limited for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Food safety risk
items.content: Canned tuna must be stored in a dry place; damaged cans can lead to spoilage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake the casserole until the top is golden brown and serve hot. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill and sprinkle extra cheese if desired. Leftovers reheat well in the microwave or on the stovetop with a splash of milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked casserole in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Whiskey is a distilled spirit made from fermented grain mash and aged in oak barrels. Major types include Scotch, Irish, American (bourbon) and Canadian whiskey. Flavors range from light and fruity to rich, smoky, and spicy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest recorded whiskey recipe dates back to 15th‑century Scotland.
The word “whiskey” comes from the Gaelic “uisge beatha,” meaning “water of life.”
Bourbon must be aged at least two years in new charred oak barrels.
Scotch whiskey is categorized into single malt and blended varieties.
In 2018, over 1.2 billion litres of Scotch whisky were sold worldwide.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols in aged whiskey may help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Moderate intake supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Studies suggest that small amounts (30–40 ml daily) can raise HDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: May lower risk of type 2 diabetes
items.content: Epidemiological data link moderate alcohol consumption with reduced diabetes risk.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Traditionally, whiskey is enjoyed as a digestif because it stimulates gastric secretions.

items.title: Social and cultural benefits
items.content: Responsible sharing can promote relaxation and improve mood.

items.title: Alcohol dependence
items.content: Regular consumption can lead to addiction and adverse health effects.

items.title: Liver disease risk
items.content: Excessive intake is associated with cirrhosis and other liver conditions.

items.title: Impaired cognition and coordination
items.content: Alcohol reduces reaction time and can increase accident risk.

items.title: Interactions with medications
items.content: Whiskey may potentiate the effects of sedatives and anticoagulants.

items.title: Caloric content
items.content: A 100 ml serving contains roughly 220 kcal, which should be considered in weight management.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Whiskey is typically served in small glasses (30–50 ml) at room temperature. It can be enjoyed neat, on the rocks, or in classic cocktails such as Old Fashioned, Manhattan, and Whiskey Sour. For tasting, a tulip‑shaped glass with a wide bowl is recommended.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bottle in a cool, dark place upright so the cork does not stay in contact with the liquid. After opening, it’s best consumed within 1–2 years, as prolonged exposure to air can alter the flavor.
